messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane is a 63-year-old publisher of Māori descent, living in a Midwestern city with his wife of forty years. Nine months ago, he attended his company’s annual holiday party at a downtown banquet hall. The evening was festive—wine and beer were poured freely, and the smell of alcohol mixed with roasted food. Then, near the kitchen, a fryer burst into flame. Within seconds thick black smoke filled the room. Tane remembers pushing through a side exit, but not before he saw a junior editor’s face lit by orange fire, frozen in terror. That image never left him.

In the weeks that followed, the memory forced its way into his mind without warning. He would be sitting at his desk and suddenly see the flames again, as clear as if he were still there. The visual memories were vivid and mostly pictorial: the smoke, the panicked crowd, the heat on his skin. He often woke from nightmares drenched in sweat, the dream residue lingering throughout the morning. The mere act of a colleague mentioning the incident at a staff meeting made his chest tighten. And any faint scent of alcohol—a whiff of wine at the grocery store, beer on someone’s breath—sent a jolt through him, instantly transporting him back to that night. And because the memory invaded so often and with such force, he began to detect its cues everywhere—the crackle of a radiator, a sudden shout outside, the burnt edge of a piece of toast—each ordinary sensation now carrying the threat of pulling him back into the smoke.

To manage these intrusions, Tane began to withdraw. He stopped accepting invitations from the friends who had been at the party, worried that talk would turn to the fire. He also changed how he moved through spaces. At home he always chose a chair with his back to the wall so he could see the entire room, and in restaurants he insisted on the same arrangement. Out of habit he started scanning every environment for signs of threat: a strange smell, an unusual sound, a door that seemed out of place. He told himself this vigilance kept him safe.

But it did not. His hypervigilance only deepened. Even inside his own living room he felt on guard, as if disaster were hiding behind the curtains. Ordinary noises—a creaking floorboard, the hum of the refrigerator—made him jump. That startle response, sharp and visceral, in turn triggered a cascade of memory: the crash of falling debris, the screaming, the heat. Each time his heart pounded, the images returned more vividly. The more alert he was, the more the past intruded on the present.

Meanwhile, his avoidance backfired. The more he stayed away from friends and colleagues, the more the memories seemed to crowd his mind during the empty hours at home. His constant scanning also made him hypersensitive to triggers: because he was always looking for danger, he noticed alcohol smells more frequently and reacted more intensely. And each time he checked his surroundings or repositioned himself with his back to a wall, he was reinforcing the belief that the world was unsafe. His alertness at home intensified; he now slept fitfully, waking at the slightest sound. The cycle tightened.

At work, his reputation as a networked publisher frayed. He turned down lunch meetings because he could not control the seating. His wife grew exasperated when he insisted on rearranging the furniture in their den so that his armchair faced the hallway. Tane understood that his reactions seemed excessive, but he was certain that relaxing his guard would invite catastrophe. It was after a quiet evening when the scent of his wife’s glass of red wine sent him into a panic—the fire replaying in his mind, the smell so real he gagged—that he finally agreed to see a therapist. What he feared most was that the images would never stop. But beneath that, he hoped for a way to sit through a dinner without watching the door.
